Team sport in which two sides of 11 players each try to score more goals than the opponent, using mainly their feet to move an inflated ball around a pitch. Commonly called football or soccer, it is played by an estimated 250 million players in over 200 countries and territories and is the world's most popular sport. Matches traditionally consist of two 45-minute halves, for a total of 90 minutes. Players may use any part of the body except the hands and arms; only goalkeepers may use their hands and arms, and only within their own penalty area. The ball is 68–70 cm in circumference, and the goal is 7.32 m wide and 2.44 m high. Depending on the competition, a tied match may be declared a draw, with 1 point to each team, or go to extra time or a penalty shoot-out.

The Laws of the Game, in effect since 1863, have been maintained by the International Football Association Board since 1886. The word "association" refers to the Football Association, founded in [[London]] in 1863, which published the first rules and coined the term to distinguish its game from other types of football, particularly [[Rugby football]]. "Soccer" derives from "-er" slang that was prevalent at the [[University of Oxford|University of Oxford]] from about 1875. The game is usually called simply football in Great Britain and most of Ulster, and soccer where other football codes prevail, such as Australia, Canada, South Africa, and the United States.

Kicking games arose independently in many cultures. The Chinese game *cuju*, recorded in the *Zhan Guo Ce* from the [[Han dynasty]], is the earliest form for which there is historical evidence; the inflatable ball was invented in the [[Tang dynasty]]. FIFA states that soccer originated in Britain from around the eighth century, and that the modern rules rest on mid-19th-century efforts to standardize the varied forms played in English public schools.

Internationally the sport is governed by [[FIFA]], under which six continental confederations operate: AFC, CAF, CONCACAF, CONMEBOL, OFC, and UEFA. The men's [[FIFA World Cup]] is the most-viewed sporting event in the world, and the final of the men's [[UEFA Champions League]] is the most-watched annual one. FIFA has faced governance controversies, including past bribery scandals that led to leadership changes. Injuries are common, averaging 6.9 per 1,000 player-participations; neuromuscular training programs such as FIFA 11+ have reduced injury rates.

Rocky, metallic, or icy minor planet that orbits within the inner Solar System or is co-orbital with a planet, as the Trojan asteroids are. Asteroids are larger than a [[Meteoroid|meteoroid]] (1 meter or larger) and are neither planets nor identified [[Comet|comets]]; a body that shows a coma when warmed by solar radiation is classed as a comet. They have no atmosphere and are broadly classified as C-type (carbonaceous), M-type (metallic), or S-type (silicaceous). Sizes range from rubble piles under a kilometer across to [[Ceres (dwarf planet)|Ceres]], a dwarf planet almost 1000 km in diameter.

Of the roughly one million known asteroids, the greatest number lie between the orbits of [[Mars]] and [[Jupiter]], approximately 2 to 4 astronomical units from the Sun, in the main [[Asteroid belt|asteroid belt]]. Their combined mass is only 3% that of Earth's Moon. Most main-belt asteroids follow slightly elliptical, stable orbits in the same direction as Earth and take three to six years to circle the Sun. They are remnants of the Solar System's formation about 4.6 billion years ago.

Ceres, discovered in 1801, was first considered a new planet. Because such bodies appeared as points of light like stars, [[William Herschel]] proposed the term asteroid, from Greek words meaning "star-like." In 2006 the International Astronomical Union introduced the broader term small Solar System body, which also covers comets, centaurs, and trans-Neptunian objects.

The Galileo spacecraft made the first close-up observation of an asteroid. [[NASA]]'s NEAR Shoemaker studied Eros, and Dawn observed Vesta and Ceres. The Japanese missions Hayabusa and Hayabusa2 returned samples of Itokawa and Ryugu, respectively. OSIRIS-REx collected a sample from Bennu in 2020 and delivered it to Earth in 2023. The Double Asteroid Redirection Test was deliberately crashed into the asteroid Dimorphos in September 2022 to test planetary defense technology. Psyche, launched in October 2023, targets a metallic asteroid; Hera, launched in October 2024, is to study the DART impact; and China's Tianwen-2, launched in May 2025, is to sample the near-Earth asteroid Kamoʻoalewa. Near-Earth asteroids could cause catastrophe if they struck Earth, as the Chicxulub impact is widely thought to have done in causing the Cretaceous–Paleogene mass extinction.

Natural science that studies celestial objects and the phenomena occurring in the cosmos. It uses mathematics, physics, and chemistry to explain the origin and evolution of planets, moons, stars, nebulae, galaxies, meteoroids, asteroids, and comets, and of phenomena such as supernova explosions, gamma ray bursts, quasars, blazars, pulsars, and cosmic microwave background radiation. More generally, it studies everything that originates beyond Earth's atmosphere. [[Cosmology]] is the branch that studies the universe as a whole. Observational astronomy collects data with telescopes, theoretical astronomy builds mathematical models, and astrometry measures the positions and motions of celestial bodies. Modern usage treats astronomy and [[Astrophysics|astrophysics]] as broadly synonymous. The word comes from the Greek *astron*, "star," and *nomos*, "law" or "rule." Unlike [[Astrology|astrology]], the belief that human affairs correlate with the positions of celestial objects, astronomy is supported by physics; the two fields share a common origin. Amateurs still play an active role, especially in discovering and observing transient events such as new comets.

Astronomy is among the oldest natural sciences. Early development was driven by practical needs such as agricultural calendars. Sites such as [[Stonehenge]] and the Nebra sky disc, and the megalithic structures at Nabta Playa in Upper Egypt, show ancient interest in the sky. The Babylonians began mathematical astronomy and found that lunar eclipses recur in the saros cycle of 223 synodic months. Greek astronomers sought rational explanations: Aristarchus of Samos proposed a heliocentric model in the 3rd century BC, and in the 2nd century BC [[Hipparchus]] catalogued 1020 stars and observed the drift now attributed to precession. The [[Antikythera mechanism]] (c. 150–80 BC) was an early analog computer for predicting the positions of the Sun, Moon, and planets. [[Ptolemy]]'s 13-volume work, known in Arabic translation as the *Almagest*, made the geocentric system the primary reference for over a thousand years.

Indian astronomers including Āryabhaṭa, Varāhamihira, and Brahmagupta integrated Greek models, and the Kerala school later refined planetary and eclipse calculations. Observatories were established in the Islamic world by the early 9th century. In 964 Abd al-Rahman al-Sufi described the Andromeda Galaxy, and the SN 1006 supernova was observed in 1006 by Ali ibn Ridwan and Chinese astronomers. In medieval Europe, Richard of Wallingford built an astronomical clock, Nicole Oresme discussed evidence for the Earth's rotation, and Jean Buridan developed the theory of impetus. [[Nicolaus Copernicus]] placed the Sun at the center in 1543, followed by Kepler's laws of planetary motion and Newton's law of universal gravitation. Space telescopes such as the Hubble Space Telescope now observe wavelengths blocked by the atmosphere.

Absence of belief in the existence of deities, contrasted with [[Theism|theism]], the belief that at least one deity exists. In the broadest sense it is simply the absence of such belief; less broadly, a rejection of the belief that any deities exist; and in the narrowest sense, the position that there are no deities. Writers disagree on how to define it, and the norm is to define it as an explicit stance against theism. Philosophers such as Antony Flew and Michael Martin distinguish positive (strong) atheism, the explicit affirmation that gods do not exist, from negative (weak) atheism, which covers all other forms of non-theism. Implicit atheism is absence of belief without conscious rejection; explicit atheism is conscious rejection. Atheism has been regarded as compatible with [[Agnosticism|agnosticism]] but also contrasted with it, and many agnostics see their view as distinct. Richard Dawkins prefers to place theist, agnostic, and atheist positions along a spectrum of theistic probability. The ancient Romans accused Christians of atheism for not worshiping the pagan deities.

Atheistic viewpoints can be traced to [[Classical antiquity]] and early Indian philosophy; Epicurus and Lucretius advanced materialist accounts that left no role for divine intervention. In the Western world atheism declined after Christianity gained prominence, then resurged in the 16th century and the [[Age of Enlightenment]], when figures such as Denis Diderot advanced atheistic arguments. It achieved a significant position worldwide in the 20th century, and estimates of those lacking theistic belief range from 500 million to 1.1 billion people. Atheist organizations have defended the autonomy of science, freedom of thought, [[Secularism|secularism]], and secular ethics.

Arguments for atheism include the lack of evidence, the problem of evil, the argument from inconsistent revelations, the rejection of concepts that cannot be falsified, and the argument from nonbelief. Nonbelievers contend that atheism is the more parsimonious position and that the burden of proof lies on the theist rather than the atheist. In some countries with apostasy or blasphemy laws, open identification as an atheist can bring imprisonment, violence, or the death penalty. Atheists elsewhere report social prejudice, and some surveys show public distrust of their morality, although cross-national studies cited by supporters find no deficit in ethical behavior. Critics of state-mandated atheism, as in the Soviet Union, point to its accompanying suppression of religion.

Second largest of the world's five oceans, an elongated, S-shaped basin lying between Europe and Africa to the east and the Americas to the west. Its area is about 85,133,000 sq km, roughly 17% of Earth's surface and 24% of its water surface. The Equator divides it into the North and South Atlantic. It connects to the Arctic Ocean in the north, the Pacific Ocean in the southwest, the Indian Ocean in the southeast, and the Southern Ocean in the south. The 20° East meridian, running south from Cape Agulhas, marks the Indian Ocean boundary. The 1953 International Hydrographic Organization definition extends the Atlantic south to Antarctica, while later maps bound it at the 60° parallel by the Southern Ocean. Including marginal seas, its coastline measures 111,866 km. Average depth is around 3,300 m.

The seafloor is split by the [[Mid-Atlantic Ridge]], a divergent tectonic boundary where new oceanic crust forms and the basin widens by 2 to 5 cm per year. The warm [[Gulf Stream]] carries heat northward along the western boundary and influences the climate of Europe and North America, and density-driven flows of deep water form part of global [[Thermohaline circulation|thermohaline circulation]]. The South Atlantic stays warm year-round, while the North Atlantic is temperate.

The name derives from [[Atlas (mythology)|Atlas]], the Titan of Greek mythology who supported the heavens. It appears in Stesichorus in the mid-sixth century BC and in the *Histories* of Herodotus around 450 BC, where it denotes the sea beyond the Strait of Gibraltar. Early Greek sailors thought the Atlantic part of Oceanus, the great river encircling all land. English cartographers later called it the Great Western Ocean.

The Norse were the first known humans to cross the Atlantic, but the 1492 expedition of [[Christopher Columbus]] proved the most consequential, opening an age of European exploration and colonization of the Americas. From the 16th to the 19th centuries the ocean was the center of the [[Atlantic slave trade]] and the [[Columbian exchange]]. Naval battles and trade grew in the early 20th century. After World War II, notable conflicts included the Cuban Missile Crisis and the Falklands War. The ocean remains a core component of world trade.

Multi-layered gas mixture, commonly called air, that surrounds the Earth's surface and is retained by gravity. It contains variable quantities of suspended aerosols and particulates that create clouds and hazes. It shields the surface from most meteoroids and ultraviolet solar radiation, reduces temperature extremes between day and night, keeps the surface warm through the [[Greenhouse effect|greenhouse effect]], redistributes heat and moisture through air currents, and provides the conditions that allow life to exist and evolve. Average surface temperature is approximately 288 K.

By mole fraction, dry air is 78.08% nitrogen, 20.95% oxygen, 0.93% argon, and 0.04% carbon dioxide, with small amounts of other trace gases, including methane, nitrous oxide, ozone, and the noble gases neon, helium, krypton, and xenon. Water vapor averages around 1% at sea level and 0.4% over the entire atmosphere, accounting for roughly 0.25% by mass. Xenon is far scarcer than the other noble gases, a puzzle known as the missing xenon problem. The average molecular weight of dry air is about 28.946 or 28.964 g/mol. Up to about 100 km, turbulence mixes the gases so that their relative concentrations stay the same; above that, in the heterosphere, lighter gases become relatively more abundant.

The primordial atmosphere was mainly hydrogen and helium accreted from the solar nebula. Atmospheric escape, volcanism and outgassing, impact events, and weathering changed it into a secondary atmosphere, dominated by nitrogen and methane, by the Archean eon. The rise of [[Cyanobacteria|cyanobacteria]], which release oxygen as a byproduct of photosynthesis, eventually converted the reducing atmosphere into an oxidative one in the Great Oxygenation Event at the end of the Archean. Further rounds of oxygenation in the Proterozoic and Phanerozoic eons produced today's nitrogen-and-oxygen atmosphere. Human activity has contributed to [[Climate change|climate change]], [[Ozone depletion|ozone depletion]], and acid deposition.

The atmosphere has a mass of about 5.15×10¹⁸ kg, three-quarters of it within about 11 km of the surface. It thins with altitude and has no definite upper boundary; the [[Kármán line]] at 100 km is often used as a conventional edge of space. Five layers are distinguished by temperature behavior: the troposphere (0–12 km), where weather occurs and air is suitable for terrestrial plants and animals; the [[Stratosphere|stratosphere]] (12–50 km), which holds the ozone layer; the mesosphere (50–80 km); the thermosphere (80–700 km); and the exosphere (700–10,000 km). The exobase varies from about 500 km to about 1,000 km depending on solar radiation. The study of the atmosphere is called [[Atmospheric science|atmospheric science]]; early pioneers include Léon Teisserenc de Bort and Richard Assmann.

Smallest unit of a chemical element that retains its chemical properties, consisting of a nucleus of protons and generally neutrons surrounded by a swarm of electrons. The number of protons distinguishes one [[Chemical element|chemical element]] from another: any atom with 11 protons is sodium, and any with 29 is copper. Atoms of the same element with different numbers of neutrons are [[Isotope|isotopes]]. Atoms are typically around 100 picometers across, so a human hair is about a million carbon atoms wide, and they are smaller than the shortest wavelength of visible light. Their behavior cannot be accurately predicted by classical physics because of quantum effects.

More than 99.94% of an atom's mass is in the nucleus. Protons carry positive charge, neutrons none, and electrons negative charge; the opposing charges bind electrons to the nucleus. An atom with equal numbers of protons and electrons is electrically neutral, while a charged atom is an [[Ion|ion]]: a negative ion (anion) has more electrons than protons, a positive ion (cation) fewer. The nuclear force holds protons and neutrons together against electromagnetic repulsion; when repulsion prevails the nucleus splits, a form of nuclear decay. Atoms attach to one another by chemical bonds to form molecules or crystals, and this ability underlies most physical changes in nature.

The word comes from the Greek *atomos*, "uncuttable," used by Leucippus and his pupil [[Democritus]] in the 5th century BC, but their idea rested on philosophical reasoning rather than scientific evidence. In the early 1800s [[John Dalton]] compiled experimental data and found the law of multiple proportions. For example, one tin oxide is 88.1% tin and 11.9% oxygen and another is 78.7% tin and 21.3% oxygen, giving oxygen amounts in a ratio of 1:2. He concluded that elements combine in multiples of a basic unit, which he called atoms.

In 1897 [[J. J. Thomson]] identified the electron. In 1911 [[Ernest Rutherford]]'s gold foil experiments revealed the nuclear structure and showed atoms to be mostly empty space. In 1913 [[Niels Bohr]] introduced electrons in fixed energy levels, and James Chadwick discovered the neutron in 1932. Quantum mechanics in the 1920s described electrons as probability clouds. Protons and neutrons are themselves made of quarks. Light elements such as hydrogen and helium were first produced in nucleosynthesis after the Big Bang about 13.8 billion years ago.

Founder of the [[Roman Empire]] and its first emperor (r. 27 BC–AD 14), also known as Octavian. Born Gaius Octavius into an equestrian family, he was the great-nephew of [[Julius Caesar]], who named him primary heir in his will. After Caesar's assassination in 44 BC he inherited the estate and took the name. In 43 BC he seized power by marching on Rome and became its youngest elected consul. With [[Mark Antony]] and Marcus Lepidus he formed a triumvirate with legally sanctioned powers to outlaw and oppose Caesar's assassins; their proscriptions eliminated political enemies. After victory at the Battle of Philippi in 42 BC they divided the [[Roman Republic]] among themselves. Octavian had Lepidus exiled in 36 BC, and his naval commander Marcus Agrippa defeated Antony at the Battle of Actium in 31 BC. Antony and [[Cleopatra]] killed themselves during the invasion of Egypt, which became Octavian's personal property.

In 27 BC the Senate granted him the honorific Augustus, "the revered." He agreed to restore the façade of a free republic centered on the Senate, magistrates, and assemblies, but control of the military and half of Rome's provinces preserved his autocratic power. Critics have described the resulting principate as autocracy disguised in republican forms. He declined to stand for reelection to the consulship, but received the powers of the tribunate and censorship, the title *princeps* ("first citizen"), and the title *pater patriae* ("father of the country"); the month of August was named after him. After Lepidus died he also became *pontifex maximus*.

Augustus annexed Egypt, Dalmatia, Pannonia, Noricum, and Raetia and completed the conquest of Hispania, though expansion suffered a major setback in Germania. He secured the frontiers with client states and peace treaties with the Parthian Empire and the Kingdom of Kush. He reformed taxation and currency, built roads with an official courier system, established a standing professional army and the Praetorian Guard, created police and fire-fighting services for Rome, and renovated much of the city. His reign began the Pax Romana, an era largely free of armed conflict. He was a writer and a patron of poets such as [[Virgil]]. He died of natural causes and the Senate deified him; rumors that his wife Livia poisoned him persist. His stepson and adoptive son [[Tiberius]] succeeded him. The principate lasted until the [[Crisis of the Third Century]].

Country, officially the Commonwealth of Australia, comprising the mainland of the Australian continent, the island of [[Tasmania]], and numerous smaller islands; capital, [[Canberra]]. Its land area is 7,688,287 sq km, making it the sixth-largest country in the world, and the continent is the flattest and driest inhabited one. It is a megadiverse country, with large central deserts and tropical rainforests along the coast.

The ancestors of [[Aboriginal Australians]] began arriving from Southeast Asia 50,000 to 65,000 years ago, during the Last Glacial Period. The Lake Mungo remains have been dated to approximately 42,000 years ago. By the time of British settlement Aboriginal Australians spoke more than 250 distinct languages, and theirs is one of the oldest living cultures in the world. Torres Strait Islanders, a distinct Melanesian people, settled their islands at least 2,500 years ago. Australia's written history began with Dutch exploration of most of the coastline in the 17th century, when the continent was called New Holland. British colonization began in 1788 with the penal colony of [[New South Wales]]. Five more self-governing British colonies followed, each gaining responsible government by 1890, and in 1901 the six federated as the Commonwealth of Australia. Autonomy from the United Kingdom increased through the Statute of Westminster Adoption Act 1942 and culminated in the Australia Act 1986.

The name derives from the Latin *Terra Australis Incognita*, "unknown southern land." Matthew Flinders popularized it after circumnavigating the continent in 1803; Governor Lachlan Macquarie recommended it in December 1817, and the British Admiralty adopted it in 1824.

Australia is a parliamentary democracy and a [[Constitutional monarchy|constitutional monarchy]], a federation of six states and ten territories. The population is highly urbanized and concentrated on the eastern seaboard; [[Sydney]] and [[Melbourne]] each have more than five million people. The country has one of the highest foreign-born populations in the world, a highly developed economy, and one of the highest per capita incomes globally, supported by abundant natural resources and trade relations. It belongs to the United Nations, the G20, the OECD, the World Trade Organization, Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation, and the [[Commonwealth of Nations]], and takes part in the security alliances ANZUS, AUKUS, and Five Eyes.

Political system characterized by the rejection of political plurality, the use of strong central power to preserve the political status quo, and reductions in [[Democracy|democracy]], [[Separation of powers|separation of powers]], [[Civil liberties|civil liberties]], and the rule of law. Authoritarian regimes may be autocratic or oligarchic and may rest on the rule of a party, the military, or a single person. States with a blurred boundary between democracy and authoritarianism are sometimes called hybrid regimes or competitive authoritarian states.

In his influential 1964 work *An Authoritarian Regime: Spain*, the political scientist Juan Linz defined authoritarianism by four qualities: limited political pluralism, achieved through constraints on the legislature, parties, and interest groups; legitimacy based on appeals to emotion and on presenting the regime as a necessary evil against problems such as underdevelopment or insurgency; minimal political mobilization, with suppression of anti-regime activity; and ill-defined executive powers used to extend the executive's reach. Minimally defined, an authoritarian government lacks free and competitive elections to legislatures, to executives, or both. Authoritarian states may maintain nominally democratic institutions such as parties, legislatures, and elections that are managed to entrench the regime and may feature fraudulent, non-competitive voting.

Power is highly concentrated and maintained by political repression and the exclusion of challengers by armed force. Rulers tend to hold "indefinite political tenure," often in a one-party state. Adam Przeworski has theorized that "authoritarian equilibrium rests mainly on lies, fear and economic prosperity." Stability depends on control over the armed forces, a bureaucracy staffed by the regime, and allegiance created through socialization and indoctrination. The transition to a more democratic form is called democratization. Unlike [[Totalitarianism|totalitarian]] systems, which seek comprehensive ideological control, authoritarian regimes tend to tolerate some private economic activity and cultural expression that does not challenge their dominance.

Constitutions in authoritarian states can serve as an "operating manual," a "billboard" signaling intent, a "blueprint" for future plans, or "window dressing" that sets out freedoms not honored in practice. Unlike democratic constitutions, they set no direct limits on executive authority. Vladimir Lenin called the Soviet Russian Constitution of 1918 a "revolutionary" document. The legal scholar Mark Tushnet distinguishes "authoritarian constitutionalist" regimes, which are dominant-party states that permit reasonably open criticism and hold elections while ensuring their own victory, from both liberal constitutionalist and purely authoritarian regimes.

The share of authoritarian states in the international system rose from 1946 until the mid-1970s and declined until 2000. Before 2000, dictatorships typically began with a coup; since then they most often arise through democratic backsliding, in which an elected leader establishes an authoritarian regime.
